_note: Original learner definitions. Patterns: first word may be inflected; one's = any possessive (my, her, their…); someone = any person word.
idioms: break the ice
to say or do something to make people feel relaxed when they first meet
He told a funny story to break the ice.
piece of cake
something very easy to do
The first question was a piece of cake.
under the weather
feeling a little ill
I'm a bit under the weather today, so I'll stay home.
hit the books
to start studying hard
Exams start next week, so I need to hit the books.
once in a blue moon
very rarely
We only eat out once in a blue moon.
cost an arm and a leg
to be very expensive
That new phone cost an arm and a leg.
get the hang of
to learn how to do something after some practice
Driving is hard at first, but you'll get the hang of it.
on the same page
agreeing about something or understanding it in the same way
Let's check we're all on the same page before we start.
call it a day
to stop working for the rest of the day
We've done enough. Let's call it a day.
beat around the bush
to avoid saying something directly
Stop beating around the bush and tell me what happened.
the ball is in one's court
it is now someone's turn to decide or act
I've made my offer. The ball is in your court.
bite off more than one can chew
to try to do more than you are able to
I bit off more than I could chew with three part-time jobs.
burn the midnight oil
to work or study late into the night
She burned the midnight oil to finish her essay.
by the skin of one's teeth
only just; by a very small amount
He passed the test by the skin of his teeth.
cut corners
to do something cheaply or quickly by ignoring rules or quality
The builders cut corners, and now the roof leaks.
get out of hand
to become difficult to control
The party got out of hand and the neighbours complained.
give someone the benefit of the doubt
to believe someone even though you are not sure
I'll give him the benefit of the doubt this time.
hit the nail on the head
to describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem
You hit the nail on the head: we need more staff.
in hot water
in trouble
He's in hot water for missing the deadline.
keep an eye on
to watch something or someone carefully
Can you keep an eye on my bag for a minute?
let the cat out of the bag
to tell a secret by mistake
She let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.
miss the boat
to lose an opportunity by being too slow
Tickets sold out in an hour. We missed the boat.
no pain no gain
you must work hard or suffer to achieve something
Training is tough, but no pain, no gain.
on thin ice
in a risky situation where you could get into trouble
After being late again, he's on thin ice with his manager.
pull someone's leg
to joke with someone by telling them something untrue
Don't worry, I'm only pulling your leg.
see eye to eye
to agree with someone
My brother and I don't always see eye to eye.
spill the beans
to tell people secret information
Come on, spill the beans! What did she say?
take it easy
to relax and not work too hard
The doctor told me to take it easy for a few days.
the last straw
the final problem that makes a situation impossible to accept
Losing my keys was the last straw after a terrible day.
under pressure
feeling stressed because of demands or worries
Students are often under pressure during exam season.
a blessing in disguise
something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good
Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.
better late than never
it is better to do something late than not at all
He finally apologised. Better late than never.
easier said than done
easy to talk about but difficult to actually do
Saving money is easier said than done.
get one's act together
to start organising yourself and behaving more effectively
You need to get your act together before the exam.
go the extra mile
to make more effort than is expected
Good teachers go the extra mile for their students.
in the long run
over a long period of time; eventually
Learning a language takes time, but it pays off in the long run.
make ends meet
to have just enough money to pay for what you need
Many families struggle to make ends meet.
off the top of one's head
without thinking carefully or checking the facts
Off the top of my head, I'd say about fifty people came.
out of the blue
suddenly and unexpectedly
An old friend called me out of the blue.
rule of thumb
a practical, general guideline
As a rule of thumb, spend two minutes planning each essay paragraph.
sit on the fence
to avoid choosing a side in an argument
You can't sit on the fence forever. Which option do you prefer?
the tip of the iceberg
a small, visible part of a much bigger problem
These complaints are just the tip of the iceberg.
think outside the box
to think creatively, in a new way
To solve this, we need to think outside the box.
up in the air
not yet decided
Our holiday plans are still up in the air.
word of mouth
information passed from person to person by talking
The restaurant became popular through word of mouth.
a drop in the ocean
a very small amount compared to what is needed
The donation was a drop in the ocean.
at the end of the day
when everything has been considered
At the end of the day, your health matters most.
back to square one
back to the beginning, with no progress
The plan failed, so we're back to square one.
catch someone's eye
to attract someone's attention
A red dress in the window caught my eye.
feel blue
to feel sad
I always feel blue on rainy Mondays.
face the music
to accept the unpleasant results of your actions
He broke the rules, and now he has to face the music.
get cold feet
to become nervous and not want to do something you planned
She got cold feet just before the interview.
have a lot on one's plate
to have many things to deal with
I have a lot on my plate at work this month.
keep in touch
to continue to communicate with someone
Let's keep in touch after the course ends.
learn the ropes
to learn how to do a job or activity
It took me a month to learn the ropes at my new job.
make up one's mind
to decide
I can't make up my mind about which course to take.
play it by ear
to decide what to do as things happen, without a plan
We don't know the weather, so let's play it by ear.
put off
to delay doing something
Don't put off your homework until Sunday night.
run out of
to use all of something so there is none left
We ran out of milk this morning.
take part in
to join an activity with other people
Over two hundred students took part in the competition.
look forward to
to feel happy and excited about something that will happen
I'm looking forward to the summer holidays.
come up with
to think of an idea or plan
She came up with a brilliant solution.
get along with
to have a friendly relationship with someone
I get along with all my classmates.
catch up on
to do something you did not have time to do earlier
I need to catch up on sleep this weekend.
deal with
to take action to solve a problem
The government must deal with rising prices.
figure out
to understand or solve something after thinking
I couldn't figure out the answer.
set up
to start a business or organisation; to arrange something
My uncle set up his own company in 2015.
turn down
to refuse an offer or request
He turned down the job because the salary was too low.
carry out
to do or complete a task, test or piece of research
The researchers carried out a survey of 500 people.
bring up
to mention a subject; to care for a child until adulthood
She brought up an interesting point in the meeting.
point out
to tell someone something they did not know or notice
The teacher pointed out a mistake in my essay.
rely on
to depend on someone or something
Many people rely on public transport to get to work.
